title: Wooden on Leadership
author: John Wooden
summary: John Wooden, who won ten NCAA titles at UCLA, explains how he led: focus on effort and preparation over winning, and teach character along with skill.
highlights: The score will take care of itself when you take care of the effort that precedes the score.

Reputation is what others perceive you as being, and their opinion may be right or wrong. Character, however, is what you really are, and nobody truly knows that but you. But you are what matters most.

title: High Output Management
author: Andrew S. Grove
summary: Intel's former CEO treats management like production: a manager's output is the output of their team, so their time should go to the work with the most leverage.
highlights: The output of a manager is the output of the organizational unit under his or her supervision or influence.
Training is quite simply one of the highest leverage activities a manager can perform.

title: Measure What Matters
author: John Doerr
summary: John Doerr explains OKRs (objectives and key results), the goal-setting system he learned from Andy Grove at Intel, with examples from Google and other companies.
highlights: “Bad companies,” Andy wrote, “are destroyed by crisis. Good companies survive them. Great companies are improved by them.”

title: Traction
author: Gino Wickman
summary: A practical system for running a small or mid-sized company, covering vision, people, data, issues, process, and getting the whole team to execute.

title: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
author: Ben Horowitz
summary: Ben Horowitz on the parts of running a company that management books skip: layoffs, firing executives, and making decisions when every option is bad.
highlights: People always ask me, “What’s the secret to being a successful CEO?” Sadly, there is no secret, but if there is one skill that stands out, it’s the ability to focus and make the best move when there are no good moves.

A healthy company culture encourages people to share bad news. A company that discusses its problems freely and openly can quickly solve them. A company that covers up its problems frustrates everyone involved.

title: Good to Great
author: Jim Collins
summary: Jim Collins and his team studied companies that went from average results to great ones and stayed there, and what set them apart from similar companies that didn't.

title: The Effective Executive
author: Peter F. Drucker
summary: Drucker describes the habits that make knowledge workers and managers effective: knowing where their time goes, focusing on contribution, building on strengths, doing first things first and making sound decisions.
highlights: People in general, and knowledge workers in particular, grow according to the demands they make on themselves.
Strong people always have strong weaknesses too.

title: The Inspiring Leader
author: John H. Zenger & Joseph Folkman
summary: Zenger and Folkman use data on thousands of leaders to show which behaviors make a leader inspiring, and how to build them.

title: Team of Rivals
author: Doris Kearns Goodwin
summary: A history of how Abraham Lincoln brought his political rivals into his cabinet and led them through the Civil War.

title: Call Sign Chaos
author: Jim Mattis & Bing West
summary: Jim Mattis on what he learned leading Marines over four decades, from commanding a platoon to running U.S. Central Command.
highlights: The first is competence. Be brilliant in the basics. Don’t dabble in your job; you must master it.
Remember: As an officer, you need to win only one battle—for the hearts of your troops. Win their hearts and they will win the fights.

title: BE 2.0
author: Jim Collins
summary: An updated edition of Collins's 1992 guide for small and mid-sized companies that want to last. It covers leadership, getting the right people, vision and values, strategy, and day-to-day execution.
highlights: How do you know if you have a truly great business? Warren Buffett has the best answer: You don’t have to hold a prayer meeting to raise prices.
Innovation often comes from seeing the relationship between unconnected ideas and melding them together.

title: The Score Takes Care of Itself
author: Bill Walsh
summary: The former 49ers coach explains how he turned a losing team into a champion by setting a standard of performance for every job in the organization, on the view that if the standards and daily habits are right, the wins follow.
highlights: Expertise coupled with strength of will is going to prevail.
No one will ever come back to you later and say "thank you" for expecting too little of them.

title: Scaling People
author: Claire Hughes Johnson
summary: A manager's handbook from Stripe's former COO on building a company's operating system as it grows: planning, hiring, team development, feedback, and communication. It pairs frameworks with templates and exercises for leaders at growing companies.
highlights: I often think of my work as a manager as clearing the path my team will need to travel. Anything that slows them down is on me.

Good communication is about providing timely and honest information, including being willing to acknowledge mistakes. People forgive mistakes, but they lose trust when information is hidden, false, or misleading, or when leadership says something but doesn’t follow through.

title: Leadership in Turbulent Times
author: Doris Kearns Goodwin
summary: A historian follows Lincoln, Theodore Roosevelt, Franklin Roosevelt, and Lyndon Johnson from early life through national crisis to show how each developed as a leader and what they did when the country needed them.
highlights: A finely developed sense of timing—knowing when to wait and when to act—would remain in Lincoln’s repertoire of leadership skills the rest of his life.
“With public sentiment, nothing can fail,” Abraham Lincoln said, “without it nothing can succeed.”

title: Only the Paranoid Survive
author: Andrew S. Grove
summary: Intel's former CEO describes strategic inflection points, the moments when a business's fundamentals change, and how leaders can recognize them early and commit to a new direction before the old one fails.
highlights: A strategic inflection point is a time in the life of a business when its fundamentals are about to change. That change can mean an opportunity to rise to new heights. But it may just as likely signal the beginning of the end.
Strategic change doesn't just start at the top. It starts with your calendar.

title: The Captain Class
author: Sam Walker
summary: A study of the most dominant teams in sports history, which finds that the common factor was not a star player or coach but a captain who did unglamorous work, held the team to a high standard, and led mostly through example and private conversation.
highlights: “You do your job so everyone around you can do their job,” Tom Brady once said. “There’s no big secret to it.”

A great leader is dedicated to doing whatever it takes to make success more likely, even if it’s unpopular, or controversial, or outrageous, or completely invisible to others. A leader has to be committed, above all else, to getting it right.

title: Who
author: Geoff Smart & Randy Street
summary: A practical hiring method: define the outcomes a role must deliver in a scorecard, source candidates through referrals, and use structured interviews to find people who can actually hit those outcomes.
highlights: “Your success as a manager is simply the result of how good you are at hiring the people around you.”
The first failure point of hiring is not being crystal clear about what you really want the person you hire to accomplish.

title: Working Backwards
author: Colin Bryar & Bill Carr
summary: Two longtime Amazon executives describe the company's management practices, including single-threaded leadership, six-page narratives, the PR/FAQ process, Bar Raiser hiring, and input metrics. They show how those practices shaped Kindle, Prime, Prime Video, and AWS.
highlights: “The best way to fail at inventing something is by making it somebody’s part-time job.”
There’s a saying often heard at Amazon: “Good intentions don’t work. Mechanisms do.”

title: What You Do Is Who You Are
author: Ben Horowitz
summary: Horowitz argues that a company's culture is defined by what its people actually do, not by stated values. He draws on examples like the Haitian revolution, the samurai, Genghis Khan, and a prison gang leader to show how leaders shape culture through their actions.
highlights: If you aren’t yourself, even you won’t follow you.
If somebody behaves in a way you can’t believe, remember that your culture somehow made that acceptable.

title: The Speed of Trust
author: Stephen M.R. Covey
summary: Covey argues that trust is a measurable factor in business: when trust is high, work moves faster and costs less. He breaks credibility into integrity, intent, capabilities and results, and lists behaviors that build or restore trust.
highlights: when trust is low, speed goes down and cost goes up. When trust is high, speed goes up and cost goes down.
Ultimately micromanagers who trust only themselves can take their companies only as far as they themselves can take them.

title: Dare to Lead
author: Brené Brown
summary: Brown applies her research on vulnerability, shame, and courage to leadership. She covers how leaders can build trust, give honest feedback, live by their values, and recover from setbacks.
highlights: Clear is kind. Unclear is unkind.
Integrity is choosing courage over comfort; it’s choosing what’s right over what’s fun, fast, or easy; and it’s practicing your values, not just professing them.

title: No Rules Rules
author: Reed Hastings & Erin Meyer
summary: Netflix's co-founder and a business professor explain the company's culture: hire very strong people, pay them well, ask for constant candid feedback, and then remove most rules and approvals so they can make their own decisions.
highlights: If you build an organization made up of high performers, you can eliminate most controls. The denser the talent, the greater the freedom you can offer.
When the boss steps out of the role of “decision approver,” the entire business speeds up and innovation increases.

title: The CEO Test
author: Adam Bryant & Kevin Sharer
summary: Drawing on interviews with hundreds of CEOs, the authors lay out the core tests of leadership: writing a simple plan, building culture and a strong team, leading change, listening, and handling a crisis.
highlights: Simplifying complexity is a leader's superpower.
Though many people are loath to admit it, except to perhaps friends, family, and trusted confidants, leadership is hellishly difficult.

title: Creativity, Inc.
author: Ed Catmull & Amy Wallace
summary: Pixar's co-founder explains how the studio protects creative work: candid feedback on early drafts, treating failure as part of the process, and managers whose job is to find and remove the hidden problems that block good people.
highlights: If you aren’t experiencing failure, then you are making a far worse mistake: You are being driven by the desire to avoid it.
Management’s job is not to prevent risk but to build the ability to recover.

title: High Growth Handbook
author: Elad Gil
summary: A guide to scaling a startup after it finds product-market fit, covering the CEO's role, hiring and managing executives, boards, culture, and company functions, with interviews from founders and operators who have done it.
highlights: A CEO’s energy levels dictate those of the team.
“You do not want to preserve culture; you want to collectively steer the right evolution of the culture.” —Patrick Collison
